what_its_for: Abatacept is used to treat moderate to severe rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis. It works by calming down your immune system to reduce joint pain, swelling, and stiffness. It may also be used in combination with other arthritis medicines.
how_to_take: Abatacept comes in two forms: an injection you give yourself under the skin (subcutaneous) using a prefilled syringe or autoinjector pen, or an intravenous (IV) infusion given by a healthcare provider in a clinic. For the self-injection form, inject it into your stomach area, front of your thighs, or outer upper arms. Rotate injection sites each time and never inject into skin that is tender, bruised, red, or hard. Let the syringe or pen warm up to room temperature for 30 minutes before injecting. Do not shake the device.
dosing: The dose depends on which form you are using and your weight. For the weekly self-injection (subcutaneous), adults typically inject 125 mg once a week on the same day each week. For the IV infusion form, your doctor will calculate your dose based on your body weight and it is given at weeks 0, 2, and 4, then once every 4 weeks after that. Always follow your doctor's specific dosing instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose of the self-injection form, inject it as soon as you remember and then continue on your regular weekly schedule. If it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and resume your normal schedule. Do not inject two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you miss an IV infusion appointment, contact your doctor or clinic right away to reschedule.
storage: Store abatacept in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Keep it in its original box to protect it from light. Do not freeze it, and do not use it if it has been frozen. If needed, the prefilled syringe or pen can be stored at room temperature (up to 77°F or 25°C) for up to 30 days, but do not put it back in the refrigerator after it has warmed up. Keep all medications out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid receiving live vaccines (such as nasal flu spray, MMR, chickenpox, or shingles vaccines) while taking abatacept, as this could cause serious infection. Talk to your doctor before getting any vaccines. Avoid close contact with people who are sick, especially with infections like colds, flu, or chickenpox, since abatacept weakens your immune system and makes it harder to fight infections. Avoid smoking, as it may make your condition worse. Let all your healthcare providers know you are taking this medicine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency care if you notice: signs of serious infection such as fever, chills, night sweats, cough, trouble breathing, burning with urination, or wounds that will not heal; signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing; signs of hepatitis such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain; unusual bruising or bleeding; or any new or worsening symptoms. Also tell your doctor if you have a history of tuberculosis (TB), cancer, or other immune conditions before starting this medicine.
when_it_works: Most people start to notice some improvement in joint pain and swelling within a few weeks, but it may take 3 to 6 months to feel the full benefit of abatacept. It is important to keep taking it even if you do not feel better right away. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Abatacept is not recommended during pregnancy unless clearly necessary. Women should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 14 weeks after the last dose. It is not known if abatacept passes into breast milk, so discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor. Elderly patients: Older adults may have a higher risk of infections and side effects. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Children: Abatacept is approved for children aged 2 years and older for juvenile idiopathic arthritis. Dosing in children is based on body weight.
